name: Vedic Mathematics (overview)
meaning: Vedic Mathematics is a system of mental calculation shortcuts compiled by Swami Bharati Krishna Tirtha (1884-1960) and published after his death in 1965 as the book 'Vedic Mathematics'. It is organised around 16 sutras (short aphorisms) and 13 sub-sutras (upa-sutras), which are applied to arithmetic, algebra, geometry and other topics. Types / main parts: (1) the 16 main sutras; (2) the 13 sub-sutras or corollaries; (3) practical techniques built from them, for example multiplication (Nikhilam, Urdhva-Tiryagbhyam), squaring (numbers ending in 5, numbers near a base), division (Paravartya Yojayet), subtraction from a power of ten, vinculum numbers, and checks such as digit sums (casting out nines) and divisibility tests. The methods themselves are ordinary, verifiable arithmetic. The claim that the sutras come from the Vedas (traditionally the Atharvaveda) is the author's own attribution and is not supported by scholarly study of the surviving Vedic texts.
whenToUse: Use this to explain what Vedic mathematics is, who compiled it, and how it is organised into sutras, sub-sutras and techniques.
source: Bharati Krishna Tirtha, Vedic Mathematics (1965); authenticity of the Vedic attribution: scholarly consensus

name: The sixteen sutras of Vedic mathematics (list)
meaning: The 16 sutras in Bharati Krishna Tirtha's book are: 1 Ekadhikena Purvena (by one more than the previous one); 2 Nikhilam Navatashcaramam Dashatah (all from 9 and the last from 10); 3 Urdhva-Tiryagbhyam (vertically and crosswise); 4 Paravartya Yojayet (transpose and apply); 5 Shunyam Samyasamuccaye (when the samuccaya is the same, it is zero); 6 (Anurupye) Shunyamanyat (if one is in ratio, the other is zero); 7 Sankalana-Vyavakalanabhyam (by addition and by subtraction); 8 Puranapuranabhyam (by the completion or non-completion); 9 Chalana-Kalanabhyam (differential calculus); 10 Yavadunam (whatever the extent of its deficiency); 11 Vyashtisamashtih (part and whole); 12 Sheshanyankena Charamena (the remainders by the last digit); 13 Sopantyadvayamantyam (the ultimate and twice the penultimate); 14 Ekanyunena Purvena (by one less than the previous one); 15 Gunitasamuccayah (the product of the sum equals the sum of the products); 16 Gunakasamuccayah (the factors of the sum equal the sum of the factors).
whenToUse: Use when asked to list or name the sutras, or how many there are.

name: Ekadhikena Purvena
meaning: Sutra 1: 'By one more than the previous one'. Its best-known use is squaring a number that ends in 5: take the part before the 5, multiply it by one more than itself, and write 25 after it. It is also used for recurring decimals of fractions with denominators ending in 9.
whenToUse: Squaring numbers that end in 5; recurring decimals of fractions such as 1/19.

name: Nikhilam Navatashcaramam Dashatah
meaning: Sutra 2: 'All from 9 and the last from 10'. It gives a quick way to subtract a number from a power of ten (subtract every digit from 9 and the last digit from 10), and the basis of the Nikhilam multiplication method for numbers close to a power of ten such as 10, 100 or 1000.
whenToUse: Subtracting from 10, 100, 1000 and so on; multiplying numbers near a power of ten.
tags: all from 9 and the last from 10

name: Urdhva-Tiryagbhyam
meaning: Sutra 3: 'Vertically and crosswise'. A general multiplication method that works for any two numbers: each column of the answer is built from the vertical and crosswise products of digits, with carries moving to the next column. The same idea is used for algebraic multiplication and in some hardware multiplier designs.
whenToUse: Multiplying any two numbers, especially when they are not near a power of ten.

name: Paravartya Yojayet
meaning: Sutra 4: 'Transpose and apply'. Used for division (especially by numbers close to a power of ten, where the divisor's complement is used as a multiplier), for dividing polynomials, and for solving certain linear equations by transposing terms.
whenToUse: Division by numbers just below a power of ten; polynomial division; solving simple equations.

name: Shunyam Samyasamuccaye
meaning: Sutra 5: 'When the samuccaya (sum or total) is the same, that samuccaya is zero'. It is a shortcut for solving certain algebraic equations in which a common total appears on both sides.
whenToUse: Solving particular kinds of algebraic equations.

name: Anurupye Shunyamanyat
meaning: Sutra 6: 'If one is in ratio, the other is zero'. Used to solve simultaneous linear equations when the coefficients of one variable are in the same ratio as the constants.
whenToUse: Simultaneous linear equations with proportional coefficients.

name: Sankalana-Vyavakalanabhyam
meaning: Sutra 7: 'By addition and by subtraction'. Used to solve simultaneous equations in which the coefficients of x and y are interchanged: add the equations and also subtract them to get simpler ones.
whenToUse: Simultaneous equations whose x and y coefficients are swapped.

name: Puranapuranabhyam
meaning: Sutra 8: 'By the completion or non-completion'. A method of completing a square or cube (or removing the need to) to simplify and solve polynomial equations.
whenToUse: Solving quadratic and higher-degree equations by completion.

name: Chalana-Kalanabhyam
meaning: Sutra 9: 'Differential calculus'. In Bharati Krishna Tirtha's book it is applied to quadratic and higher equations, using ideas related to differentiation.
whenToUse: Solving certain polynomial equations; links to differential calculus.

name: Yavadunam
meaning: Sutra 10: 'Whatever the extent of its deficiency'. Used to square and cube numbers near a power of ten: find how far the number is from the base (the deficiency or excess), then the answer is the number plus that deviation, followed by the square of the deviation.
whenToUse: Squares and cubes of numbers near 10, 100, 1000.

name: Vyashtisamashtih
meaning: Sutra 11: 'Part and whole'. Used in algebra, for example to treat expressions part by part and then as a whole when factorising or solving.
whenToUse: Factorisation and algebra problems that can be handled part by part.

name: Sheshanyankena Charamena
meaning: Sutra 12: 'The remainders by the last digit'. Used to find the recurring decimal expansion of fractions such as 1/7 by repeatedly using remainders.
whenToUse: Recurring decimals of fractions.

name: Sopantyadvayamantyam
meaning: Sutra 13: 'The ultimate and twice the penultimate'. Used in solving certain algebraic and fractional equations.
whenToUse: Certain algebraic equations involving fractions.

name: Ekanyunena Purvena
meaning: Sutra 14: 'By one less than the previous one'. Used to multiply by numbers made only of nines such as 9, 99, 999: the left part of the answer is the other number minus 1, and the right part is its complement from 9s.
whenToUse: Multiplying by 9, 99, 999 and similar numbers.

name: Gunitasamuccayah
meaning: Sutra 15: 'The product of the sum is equal to the sum of the products'. Used to check the correctness of products and other results by comparing digit sums or values.
whenToUse: Verifying results of multiplication and factorisation.

name: Gunakasamuccayah
meaning: Sutra 16: 'The factors of the sum is equal to the sum of the factors'. Used in factorisation, to check factors of algebraic expressions.
whenToUse: Checking factorisation of expressions.

name: Nikhilam multiplication (numbers near a base)
meaning: A multiplication shortcut for two numbers close to a power of ten (10, 100, 1000). Write each number's deviation from the base. The left part of the answer is either number plus the other's deviation (cross-add). The right part is the product of the two deviations, written with as many digits as the base has zeros (carry or borrow into the left part if needed). It is exact because A x B = Base x (A + y) + x x y, where x and y are the deviations.
whenToUse: Both numbers are close to 10, 100, 1000 or another power of ten.
steps: Pick the base (power of ten) nearest to both numbers.
Write the deviation of each number from the base (negative if below).
Left part: one number plus the other's deviation.
Right part: multiply the two deviations; it must have as many digits as the base has zeros.
Join left | right (carry or borrow if the right part is too big or negative).
examples: 98 x 97: base 100, deviations -2 and -3. Left 98-3 = 95. Right (-2)(-3) = 06. Answer 9506.
88 x 77 = 6776 (right part 276 carries 2 to the left)

name: Urdhva-Tiryagbhyam multiplication (general)
meaning: A multiplication method that works for any two numbers. Pad both numbers to the same number of digits. Working from the right, each column of the answer is the sum of the products of all digit pairs whose positions add up to that column: the vertical product in the first and last columns, and the crosswise products in between. Write the units digit of each column total and carry the rest to the next column.
whenToUse: Any multiplication, especially when the numbers are not close to a power of ten.
steps: Write the numbers one under the other with the same number of digits (pad with zeros).
Column 1: multiply the right-most digits.
Next columns: add the cross products of digit pairs, plus any carry.
Write the last digit of each column total and carry the rest.
Read the digits from the last column back to the first.
examples: 23 x 14: column 1: 3x4 = 12, write 2 carry 1. Column 2: 2x4 + 3x1 = 11, +1 = 12, write 2 carry 1. Column 3: 2x1 = 2, +1 = 3. Answer 322.

name: Squaring numbers ending in 5
meaning: For a number written as P5 (P is the part before the final 5), the square is P x (P+1) followed by 25. This works because (10P + 5) squared = 100 P(P+1) + 25.
whenToUse: Squaring any number that ends in 5.
steps: Remove the final 5 to get P.
Compute P x (P + 1).
Write 25 after it.
source: VedaSutra curated notes (verified algebra; matches the solver in server/services/solver)

name: Squaring numbers near a base
meaning: For a number N close to a power of ten B, let d = N - B. Then N squared = (N + d) followed by d squared, where d squared is written with as many digits as B has zeros (carry into the left part if it is bigger). It follows from N^2 = B(N + d) + d^2.
whenToUse: Squaring numbers close to 10, 100, 1000.
steps: Find d = N - base.
Left part: N + d.
Right part: d squared, with as many digits as the base has zeros.
Join the parts.
examples: 88 squared: d = -12; left 76; right 144 carries 1, so 77 | 44 = 7744

name: Vinculum numbers
meaning: Vinculum notation rewrites a digit above 5 as a negative (barred) digit by borrowing from the next place on the left: a digit d becomes (10 - d) barred and 1 is added to the digit on its left. For example 68 = 1 3̄ 2̄, meaning 100 - 30 - 2. Small digits make some multiplications and subtractions easier. The notation is ordinary place-value arithmetic with negative digits.
whenToUse: Simplifying numbers with large digits (6-9) before calculating.
steps: Work from the right.
A digit above 5 becomes (10 - digit) with a bar, and 1 is carried to the next digit on the left.
Repeat; a final carry becomes a leading 1.

name: Digit sum and casting out nines (Navashesha)
meaning: The digit sum (digital root) of a number is found by adding its digits repeatedly until one digit remains; it equals the remainder on division by 9 (using 9 when the remainder is 0). Because of this, the digit sum of a product equals the digit sum of the product of the digit sums, which gives a quick check on multiplication. A mismatch proves the answer is wrong; a match does not prove it is right.
whenToUse: Checking the result of a multiplication, addition or subtraction quickly.
steps: Find the digit sum of each number.
Multiply the digit sums and reduce again.
Compare with the digit sum of the claimed answer.
source: VedaSutra curated notes (verified arithmetic; matches the solver in server/services/solver)

name: Divisibility rules
meaning: Quick digit-based tests: by 2 (last digit even); 3 (digit sum divisible by 3); 4 (last two digits divisible by 4); 5 (ends in 0 or 5); 6 (divisible by 2 and 3); 7 (remove the last digit and subtract twice it from the rest, repeat); 8 (last three digits divisible by 8); 9 (digit sum divisible by 9); 10 (ends in 0); 11 (difference between the sum of digits in odd places and in even places is a multiple of 11).
whenToUse: Checking whether a number divides evenly without dividing.
examples: 1001 by 7: 100 - 2x1 = 98, which is 14 x 7, so yes
